d: The cockcrow, as a period of time, between midnight and 3 a.m.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “crowing” or “crowing of a rooster.” It refers specifically to the sound made by a rooster, rather than to the bird itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Mark 13:35. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the rooster’s crowing. This gives the word a clear, concrete reference to a familiar sound.

This word means “rest”: relief from weariness, disturbance, or ongoing activity. It is a noun describing a condition of repose or release rather than an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Matthew, Luke, and Revelation. Its basic meaning remains “rest” across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to relief sought, a place of repose, or the absence of rest. The word appears in Matthew 11:29, Matthew 12:43, Luke 11:24, Revelation 4:8, and Revelation 14:11.

This word means “unbelief,” describing the absence or failure of faith. It refers to not believing what God has said or what is being proclaimed, though its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times in 11 verses, including passages in Matthew, Mark, Romans, and Hebrews. The word can describe unbelief as a condition or response rather than an action by itself.

This word means “silversmith,” a person who makes or works with objects made of silver. It functions as a noun, naming someone by his occupation rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:24. The word itself identifies the trade; the surrounding verse and passage determine what this particular silversmith was doing or why he is mentioned.

d: (originally: a little lamb, but diminutive force was lost), a lamb.

e.t: This word means “lamb,” referring to a young sheep. It is used as an ordinary noun for a lamb, as in John 21:15, and it appears repeatedly in Revelation, where the word continues to identify a lamb within the vision’s language. The Greek New Testament uses this word 30 times in 28 verses, with 29 occurrences in Revelation and one in John. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it occurs; the surrounding verse determines what the lamb is doing or how it relates to the passage.

d: Head of a custom-house, chief tax-gatherer or publican.

e.t: This word refers to a chief tax collector—a person who held a leading role in collecting taxes. It identifies the person’s occupation and position rather than describing an action or feeling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:2. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself directly names a tax collector with chief responsibility or rank.

e.t: This word means “to foam” or “to foam at the mouth.” It describes froth or bubbles forming at a person’s mouth, and functions as a verb describing that physical action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Mark 9:18 and Mark 9:20. These occurrences use the word for visible foaming at the mouth, while the broader significance of the surrounding episode belongs to the verse and passage context rather than to the word’s basic meaning itself.

This word refers to a person’s lifestyle—the way that person lives. It describes life as a continuing pattern or manner of living, rather than a single action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:4, so its precise emphasis there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense is a person’s established way of life or daily conduct.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “remained,” “to remain,” or “to stay.” It describes continuing in a place rather than leaving, whether for a short period or longer. As a verb, it can describe people staying in a location or continuing there during their work and travel. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, with eight occurrences in Acts and one in John. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is remaining in place.

d: To cut in two, perhaps: scourge severely.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to cut in two” or “to cut to pieces.” It describes a decisive act of dividing something apart, rather than merely marking or separating it gently. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Matthew 24:51 and Luke 12:46. Both occurrences use the same central idea of cutting apart. The precise force of the word in either verse is clarified by its surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an act of cutting something into pieces or two distinct parts.

This word means “to classify”: to place someone or something into a considered category or assessment. It describes an act of judging or sorting rather than merely noticing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 10:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic meaning is the act of making a classification or assessment.

d: In the manner of Gentiles, like the rest of the world.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “Gentile-like” or “like a Gentile.” It describes conduct or manner that resembles that of a Gentile, rather than naming a person directly. Its meaning is concerned with how someone acts or presents himself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 2:14. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of the word there, but its basic sense is behavior that is Gentile-like.

d: From out, out from among, from, suggesting from the interior outwards.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “from,” “of,” or “out of.” It marks origin, source, or the point from which someone or something comes. Depending on the sentence, it can connect a person or thing with its source, or describe movement away from a place or position. It is a very common word, occurring 914 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise sense is determined by the surrounding words.

“To spit out” or “to vomit” means to expel something from the mouth or stomach. This Greek New Testament verb pictures forceful rejection, not merely speaking or allowing something to fall away. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Revelation 3:16. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on its surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself plainly describes something being expelled.

This word means “ninth” and can describe the ninth hour of the day. It is an ordinal word, identifying something as number nine in sequence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times and is used especially in expressions marking a time of day. Its meaning remains a straightforward designation of the ninth position or hour; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being counted or timed.

The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic meaning appears across several kinds of passages. e.t: This word means “it is legal” or “it is permitted.” It is an expression used to say that an action is allowed, lawful, or acceptable under a stated authority or standard. In the Greek New Testament, it often appears in questions about whether someone may do something, making permission the central idea rather than ability or opportunity. It occurs 31 times in the Greek New Testament, across 29 verses, so its precise force in a sentence depends on what action or rule is being discussed.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to fall,” “to fall upon,” or “to press upon.” It describes movement or pressure coming down on or against someone or something. The exact English wording can depend on the sentence, but its central idea is an advance that bears upon another person or object. It occurs 11 times in 11 New Testament verses, with six occurrences in Acts and two in Luke. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: (literal: to draw over), to become as uncircumcised.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, iMperative, third, Singular

e.t: This verb means “to conceal circumcision” or “to uncircumcise,” describing an attempt to hide or undo the physical mark of circumcision. It refers specifically to changing how circumcision is outwardly presented, rather than naming circumcision itself. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 7:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns concealing or reversing circumcision.

d: Zebulun, one of the sons of Jacob, and founder of one of the twelve tribes.

e.t: Zebulun is a personal and tribal name carried into the New Testament from Israel’s scriptural history. It identifies Zebulun rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears three times: twice in Matthew and once in Revelation. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its reference to Zebulun. The word is consistently rendered “Zebulun.”

This word means “summer,” the warm season of the year. It is a noun used to name that season directly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each time in a saying that refers to recognizable seasonal signs. The word itself simply identifies summer; its fuller significance in any passage comes from the surrounding words and situation. It appears in Matthew 24:32, Mark 13:28, and Luke 21:30, with each occurrence rendered “summer.”

d: A horse-soldier, a mounted soldier, a cavalryman.

e.t: This word means “horseman,” referring to a person who rides a horse, especially as part of a mounted military force. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 23, in connection with the Roman troops assigned to move Paul safely. The word therefore identifies mounted soldiers rather than infantry. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines the specific duties these horsemen performed in that situation.

me: Verb, Present, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to be clearly seen,” “to have been perceived,” or “to perceive.” It describes something that can be recognized plainly rather than remaining hidden or indistinct. The word focuses on clear perception—seeing or understanding something sufficiently for it to be noticed. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 1:20, so its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To trample down, trample under foot, spurn.

e.t: This word means “to trample”—to tread on something with the feet, often conveying forceful or contemptuous treatment. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, so its basic sense is focused and consistent across its uses. The surrounding words determine whether it refers to literal trampling or uses that physical action to express a serious attitude toward something treated as worthless or dishonored.

d: Corinth, in north-east Peloponnese, the capital of the Roman province Achaia.

e.t: Corinth is the name of a city. In the Greek New Testament, this word identifies Corinth as a place connected with events and people mentioned in Acts, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, and 2 Timothy. It occurs six times in six verses, including references to Paul’s movements, the Corinthian believers, and a person or situation associated with that city. As a proper place name, its meaning is geographical rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality.

This word describes something costly or rich—something valuable, luxurious, or associated with abundance. It functions as a describing word rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 18:14. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise reference in that passage must be understood from its immediate context. Its central idea remains the quality of being expensive, richly supplied, or materially splendid.

d: To change; to change my mind.
me: Verb, second Aorist, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to change mind” or “to change one's mind.” It describes a person’s change in thinking or judgment, rather than merely a passing feeling. In its one occurrence in the Greek New Testament, it functions as an expression of altered inner judgment. The precise force in Acts 28:6 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains a reversal or change of mind.

d: To ask in marriage; pass: to be betrothed.

e.t: This word means “to be pledged to marriage” or “to betroth.” It describes the relationship or action connected with a marriage commitment made before the wedding itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Matthew and Luke, in references concerning Mary and Joseph’s relationship. The word therefore points to a recognized promise or commitment to marry, rather than simply a general association between a man and woman. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To rob; to set apart for oneself, appropriate for my own benefit, purloin.

e.t: This word means “to embezzle” or “to hold back for oneself.” It describes taking or retaining something that should be given, surrendered, or entrusted to another person. In the New Testament, it occurs three times, all in the Greek New Testament: twice in Acts and once in Titus. Its basic sense concerns dishonest withholding rather than simply saving or keeping something lawfully. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word consistently points to taking for oneself what is not rightfully one’s own.

Lust is a word for strong, uncontrolled sexual desire. It names an inward craving rather than a mere physical action, so it describes what a person wants or desires. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Romans 1:27. The English rendering is “lust,” matching its central meaning. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

d: To enter secretly, come in from the side.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “came in” or “to come in,” describing someone or something entering. It presents coming into a place, situation, or sphere rather than merely remaining outside. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Romans and once in Galatians. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea is entry or arrival into something.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “even more” or “superabundantly,” expressing an amount or degree that goes beyond what is ordinary or already stated. It functions as an intensifying adverb, strengthening the description of an action, condition, or extent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is consistent but its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding words and passage. It appears in Matthew, Mark, and Acts.

d: A covetous or avaricious person; one desirous of having more.

e.t: This word refers to a “greedy person”—someone driven by the desire to gain more, especially for personal advantage. It describes a person characterized by grasping self-interest rather than contentment. The word focuses on the person’s controlling desire, not simply on owning possessions or having wealth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning remains a person ruled by greed.

This word means “river,” referring to a natural stream of flowing water. It can describe one river or more than one, as shown by the related plural meaning “rivers.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times across 17 verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its ordinary sense remains a literal river, whether mentioned in a geographical setting or used within a larger scene. The surrounding verse determines the particular river being discussed, but the word itself identifies the flowing body of water.

Samuel is a personal name referring to the prophet and judge Samuel known from Israel’s history. As a name, it identifies the same biblical person rather than describing a quality, action, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears three times: twice in Acts and once in Hebrews. These references preserve Samuel’s place among the prophets and faithful people remembered in Scripture, but the name itself simply identifies him. Its specific significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “legs,” referring to the legs of a person. It is a plural noun used for the physical body part. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in John 19:31–33, and each occurrence is rendered “legs.” The word itself identifies the body part without, by itself, expressing an emotion, virtue, command, or spiritual quality. Its precise significance in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “perfection.” It refers to a state of complete fulfillment or wholeness, expressing the idea of something brought to its full measure. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Luke and once in Hebrews. Its central meaning remains the same in both occurrences: perfection as the goal or condition of complete realization, while the surrounding verse determines its precise emphasis.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts, so its recorded use is limited to that corpus and book. The surrounding verse determines who is serving and what the service involves, but the word itself centers on active service or assistance.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears 10 times across 9 verses, so its basic sense is consistent even though its particular force depends on the surrounding sentence. It is used as an action word describing what someone chooses to do or not do toward another.

d: A commander of a thousand men, a military tribune.

e.t: This word means “military officer,” referring to a person holding authority within a military force. It is a noun used for an official military role rather than for soldiers generally. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 21 times, with most occurrences in Acts, where such officers appear in connection with Roman military authority. The word also appears in Mark, John, and Revelation, showing that it can describe a recognized officer across several kinds of scenes.
